snapshot.title: SSC Quant: Data Interpretation (DI)
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC Quant Finale Hook: 360: 100%. 1%: 3.6. DI: Perc+Ratio+Avg. Approx for speed. Read units carefully.

quick_notes.title: Pie Chart Trick
quick_notes.detail: 360° : 100%. So, 3.6° : 1%. To convert degrees to %, divide by 3.6. To convert % to degrees, multiply by 3.6.
quick_notes.explanation: A pie chart is a circular graph that shows how a whole amount is divided into parts, like slices of a pie. The full circle of a pie chart is 360 degrees, and this represents the total, which is 100 percent of the data. This means that every 3.6 degrees on the chart equals 1 percent of the total. To change a number given in degrees into a percentage, you divide that number by 3.6. To change a percentage into degrees, you multiply that percentage by 3.6. For example, if a slice of the pie is 36 degrees, that slice represents 10 percent of the total because 36 divided by 3.6 equals 10.

quick_notes.title: Bar & Line Graphs
quick_notes.detail: Read the axes carefully. Watch for the units (thousands, lakhs, millions). Usually involves Percentage Change or Averages.
quick_notes.explanation: A bar graph uses rectangular bars to compare different amounts, while a line graph uses connected points to show how something changes over time. To understand either graph, you must first look at the two axes: the horizontal axis (the line running left to right) and the vertical axis (the line running up and down); these axes show what information is being displayed and what numbers are used. Always check the unit label on the axes, because numbers might be written in thousands (meaning each number is 1,000), in lakhs (an Indian unit meaning 100,000), or in millions (1,000,000), so you need to multiply correctly to get the real value. The questions often ask you to find the percentage change, which is how much a number increases or decreases compared to its original value, or to calculate an average, which is adding up several numbers and then dividing by how many numbers you added.

quick_notes.title: Tabular DI
quick_notes.detail: Most common in CGL Tier 2. Requires fast addition and subtraction. Focus on row/column totals.
quick_notes.explanation: Tabular DI stands for Tabular Data Interpretation, which is a type of math question where information is given in a table with rows and columns. CGL Tier 2 refers to the second stage of the SSC Combined Graduate Level exam, a government job test in India. In these questions, you need to quickly add numbers across rows or down columns and subtract to find missing values or differences. The main trick is to always check the totals for each row and each column because those sums help you solve the problem step by step.

quick_notes.title: Ratio & Comparison
quick_notes.detail: Comparing growth rates or finding ratios between different years/categories.
quick_notes.explanation: A ratio is a way to compare two numbers or quantities by showing how many times one number contains the other, for example writing 3:2 means for every 3 of one thing there are 2 of another. To compare growth rates, you look at how much something increases over time, like the percentage increase from one year to the next, and then you can compare those rates between different years to see which year had faster growth. Similarly, you can find ratios between different categories, such as the number of boys to girls in a class, by writing their counts as a fraction and simplifying it. This helps you understand relationships between numbers without needing actual large values, just the relative size. Always remember that a ratio is expressed in simplest form, and when comparing growth rates, you must use the same time period for each rate to make a fair comparison.

quick_notes.title: Approximation
quick_notes.detail: Don't calculate exact values if options are far apart. Round off numbers (e.g., 543 to 540) for speed.
quick_notes.explanation: Approximation means finding a number that is close to the exact value but easier to work with. This method is useful in exams like the Staff Selection Commission (SSC) when the answer choices are far apart. For example, you can round off a number like 543 to 540 to simplify calculations; rounding off means replacing a number with a simpler number that is approximately equal. By using approximation, you save time without needing to compute exact values. Always check that the options are sufficiently distant to avoid mistakes.
